title: Neither coming nor going
hookLine: a sphere where there is no earth, water, fire or wind, no coming or going
last: BECAUSE THERE IS, AN ESCAPE IS KNOWN.

lines: A LIST OF WHAT ISN'T THERE.
cards: Try to describe silence without mentioning sound. Or darkness without mentioning light. It's almost impossible; people describe things by what's in them.

The first discourse of the Udana's last chapter takes on an even harder job. The Buddha is instructing the monks about nibbana, and the text says they listen with their whole minds, paying close attention, ears open.
What he gives them is not a description. It's a list of everything that isn't there.

teach.b: There is, monks, that sphere, he says, where there is no earth, no water, no fire, no wind. Those four elements were the ancient way of naming everything solid, liquid, hot and moving: everything physical.
None of it there. Then he goes further.

Not the sphere of infinite space, not infinite consciousness, not nothingness, not neither-perception-nor-non-perception: the four formless states the texts describe, very subtle places a meditating mind can reach.
Not those either. Not this world, not another world, not sun, not moon.

teach.h: NO COMING, NO GOING, NO STAYING.
teach.b: There, he says, there is no coming, no going, no staying, no passing away, no arising. It has no support, no movement, no basis.
This, just this, is the end of dukkha. Yesterday's saying named the unborn.

Today's empties out every place you might look for it, from the ground under your feet to the highest heaven of the mind. And then, after all those nots, one word of yes: this is the end of suffering.
Theravada teachers read the passage as describing nibbana, which isn't a place in the ordinary sense, even though the text calls it a sphere.

how: This passage is often read in Theravada teaching on nibbana, and some meditation teachers cite it when explaining that the goal is not a meditative state or a heavenly place.

o: a sphere, a base or dimension

games.q: neither coming nor going: tap the pairs.

s: the passage says nibbana is the highest meditative state
it sets aside even the four formless states.
the monks are described as listening with their whole minds
attentive, ears open, as the text says.
the passage ends by naming it the end of dukkha
after all the negatives: this, just this, is the end of suffering.

games.q: you're a monk listening to the Buddha. he's just said that in this sphere there is no earth, water, fire or wind. what does he say next?
o: but there are the formless states of meditation.
nor the formless states, nor this world, nor another; no coming or going.
it is a heaven above the gods.
games.why: he sets aside even the subtlest states, and this world and the next. then: this, just this, is the end of dukkha.

practice: Give the listening your whole mind, the way the monks did, ears open. A sound arrives; follow it until it ends, then the next, noticing that each has a coming and a going, and a gap between.
Don't fill the gap with a thought; just keep listening, without reaching for anything.

wordCard.voice: Ayatana, a sphere or base. The Udana's words for nibbana: no earth, water, fire or wind; no coming, going or staying; just this, the end of dukkha. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali ayatana: a sphere, a base, a dimension. the passage begins 'there is that ayatana'.

carryVoice: Your line: the end of dukkha. After all the nots, one plain yes. See you tomorrow.
